evidence.excerpt: Standard Wright's law assumes that cumulative average unit cost declines indefinitely as a power function of cumulative output, but in high-mix low-volume contract manufacturing the workforce frequently switches between product types, limiting the depth of learning achievable before a product is discontinued. This paper tests whether a plateau-modified learning curve, which introduces an asymptotic cost floor parameter, fits ramp-up data better than the standard two-parameter model in such environments. A dataset of 22 product ramp-ups from a medical device sub-assembly contractor was used. Model comparison was performed using corrected Akaike information criterion. The plateau model produced a lower AICc in 16 of 22 cases, with the improvement being statistically meaningful in 11 cases based on a likelihood-ratio test at the 0.05 level. The estimated plateau was reached on average at 340 cumulative units, which in this factory corresponded to roughly eight to twelve weeks of production. The paper concludes that the plateau model is preferable when typical production runs are short, and provides a simple heuristic for practitioners to choose between the two formulations based on expected run length.
